original_value: Shape sensing is one of most crucial components of typical structural health monitoring systems and has become a promising technology for future large-scale engineering structures to achieve significant improvement in their safety, reliability, and affordability. The inverse finite element method (iFEM) is an innovative shape-sensing technique that was introduced to perform three-dimensional displacement reconstruction of structures using in situ surface strain measurements. Moreover, isogeometric analysis (IGA) presents smooth function spaces such as non-uniform rational basis splines (NURBS), to numerically solve a number of engineering problems, and recently received a great deal of attention from both academy and industry. In this study, we propose a novel “isogeometric iFEM approach” for the shape sensing of thin and curved shell structures, through coupling the NURBS-based IGA together with the iFEM methodology. The main aim is to represent exact computational geometry, simplify mesh refinement, use smooth basis/shape functions, and allocate a lower number of strain sensors for shape sensing. For numerical implementation, a rotation-free isogeometric inverse-shell element (isogeometric Kirchhoff–Love inverse-shell element (iKLS)) is developed by utilizing the kinematics of the Kirchhoff–Love shell theory in convected curvilinear coordinates. Therefore, the isogeometric iFEM methodology presented herein minimizes a weighted-least-squares functional that uses membrane and bending section strains, consistent with the classical shell theory. Various validation and demonstration cases are presented, including Scordelis–Lo roof, pinched hemisphere, and partly clamped hyperbolic paraboloid. Finally, the effect of sensor locations, number of sensors, and the discretization of the geometry on solution accuracy is examined and the high accuracy and practical aspects of isogeometric iFEM analysis for linear/nonlinear shape sensing of curved shells are clearly demonstrated.

result.paraphrase: Shape sensing is a key element of conventional structural health monitoring systems and is emerging as a promising method for future large-scale engineering structures to improve safety, reliability, and affordability. The inverse finite element method (iFEM) is an innovative shape-sensing technique originally introduced for three-dimensional displacement reconstruction of structures from in situ surface strain measurements. In addition, isogeometric analysis (IGA) provides smooth function spaces such as non-uniform rational basis splines (NURBS) for numerical solution of many engineering problems and has recently attracted considerable attention from academia and industry. In this study, we propose a new “isogeometric iFEM approach” for shape sensing of thin and curved shell structures by coupling NURBS-based IGA with iFEM. The main objective is to preserve exact computational geometry, simplify mesh refinement, use smooth basis/shape functions, and reduce the number of strain sensors required for shape sensing. For numerical implementation, a rotation-free isogeometric inverse-shell element (isogeometric Kirchhoff–Love inverse-shell element (iKLS)) is developed based on the kinematics of Kirchhoff–Love shell theory in convected curvilinear coordinates. Accordingly, the proposed isogeometric iFEM methodology minimizes a weighted-least-squares functional using membrane and bending section strains, in agreement with classical shell theory. Several validation and demonstration cases are presented, including the Scordelis–Lo roof, pinched hemisphere, and partly clamped hyperbolic paraboloid. Finally, the influence of sensor placement, the number of sensors, and geometric discretization on solution accuracy is investigated, clearly demonstrating the high accuracy and practical advantages of isogeometric iFEM analysis for linear and nonlinear shape sensing of curved shells.
